slides.title: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis
slides.eyebrow: Body fluids and sputum · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Cerebrospinal fluid (lumbar puncture, usually 1–5 mL)  ·  Units: mg/dL, g/L, mmol/L

What it is used for: CSF analysis helps diagnose diseases of the central nervous system: infections (meningitis, encephalitis), autoimmune disorders (Guillain-Barré syndrome, multiple sclerosis), bleeding in the brain, tumors (including cancer that has spread) and Alzheimer disease. Signs of infection include fever, severe headache, seizures, stiff neck, nausea and vomiting, sensitivity to light, double vision, behaviour changes and confusion.

slides.title: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis
slides.eyebrow: Body fluids and sputum · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: CSF is a clear, colourless, watery fluid that flows in and around the brain and spinal cord. It cushions them against sudden impact and removes waste products from the brain. Diseases of the brain and spinal cord can change the amount or make-up of CSF.

CSF analysis is a group of tests: cell count, total protein, glucose, chloride, lactate dehydrogenase, oligoclonal bands, cancer cells (cytology), opening pressure, cryptococcal antigen, viral antibodies and DNA, and bacteria (including VDRL for syphilis). Gram staining sorts bacteria by colour and shape into Gram-positive and Gram-negative.

slides.title: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis
slides.eyebrow: Body fluids and sputum · Interpreting the result · 1/2
bullets: MedlinePlus gives these example normal values (they vary by lab — use the reference on your report): cells 0–5 white blood cells (all mononuclear) and 0 red blood cells; glucose 50–80 mg/dL (2.77–4.44 mmol/L) or more than two-thirds of the blood sugar level; protein 15–60 mg/dL (0.15–0.6 g/L); opening pressure 90–180 mm of water; no bacteria grow in culture and no cancer cells are present.

Raised protein may be a sign of a tumor, bleeding, nerve inflammation, infection or injury; a blockage in CSF flow causes protein to build up rapidly in the lower spinal area. Low protein can mean CSF is being produced rapidly or there is a more general protein deficiency.

slides.title: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis
slides.eyebrow: Body fluids and sputum · Interpreting the result · 2/2
bullets: Abnormal glucose may be due to high blood sugar, infection (bacterial or fungal), inflammation of the central nervous system or a tumor. CSF glucose is affected by blood glucose, especially at extreme levels, so it is compared with blood glucose.

Abnormal results have many causes: meningitis due to bacteria, fungus, tuberculosis or a virus, encephalitis, multiple sclerosis, cancer, hepatic encephalopathy, high blood sugar and others. Results depend on which tests were done, and more tests are usually needed to confirm a diagnosis.

slides.title: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis
slides.eyebrow: Body fluids and sputum · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/2
bullets: Pre-analytics: The sample is usually taken by lumbar puncture: after local anesthetic, a thin hollow needle is inserted between two lower vertebrae and 1–5 mL of CSF is withdrawn. Rarely, cisternal or ventricular puncture or a shunt or drain is used. The patient must stay still; lying on the back for an hour or two afterwards may help prevent a headache.
No special preparation is needed, but you may be asked to empty your bladder and bowels first. Tell the provider about all medicines, especially blood thinners, aspirin and herbal remedies.

slides.title: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis
slides.eyebrow: Body fluids and sputum · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/2
bullets: Limitations: Some infections, such as bacterial meningitis, are life-threatening emergencies; treatment may be started before a final diagnosis.
Normal ranges vary between laboratories, and some labs use different units or test different specimens — discuss your result with your provider.

slides.title: Cerebrospinal fluid: formation and functions
bullets: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) is a biological fluid needed for brain tissue to work properly and different from the body’s other fluids; it forms in the brain ventricles by ultrafiltration of blood plasma through vessel walls and passes into the subarachnoid spaces of the brain and spinal cord.
From the subarachnoid space it passes into the subdural space and is absorbed into the blood through small vessels.

Excretory role: the brain has no lymphatic system, so products of brain metabolism leave through the capillary bloodstream and the CSF; many drugs and metabolites enter the CSF and are quickly removed.

slides.title: Cerebrospinal fluid: formation and functions
bullets: Transport role: carrying substances from one part of the brain to another, transporting biologically active substances and hormones.
The ionic composition of CSF (K⁺, H⁺, HCO₃⁻, Ca, Mg and others) affects breathing, blood pressure and heart rate; CSF also gives mechanical protection.
CSF is renewed several times a day according to the body’s needs.

slides.title: Collecting CSF and macroscopic examination
bullets: The routine clinical analysis of CSF must be done within 3 hours of obtaining the biomaterial; CSF is obtained by lumbar puncture, suboccipital puncture or during surgery.
The first 5 drops are discarded and the rest is collected into 3 tubes: 1 for biochemistry, 2 for cytology, 3 for observing a fibrin film or clot.

Normally CSF is colourless and looks like water (its colour is compared with distilled water in a tube of the same size). Red colour comes from admixed blood (erythrocytarchia); pink, yellow or brown (xanthochromia) from oxyhaemoglobin, methaemoglobin and bilirubin; the intensity of xanthochromia is recorded on a four-plus scale.

slides.title: Collecting CSF and macroscopic examination
bullets: Green colour comes from oxidation of bilirubin to biliverdin; turbid yellow-green colour is seen in purulent meningitis or rupture of a brain abscess.
Clarity: turbidity is linked to erythrocytes, leukocytes, other cellular elements, growth of microorganisms or raised protein.
Fibrin film: if tuberculous meningitis is suspected and no film forms at once, the CSF is left for a day at room temperature without shaking; if erythrocytes are plentiful no film forms.

slides.title: CSF biochemistry and microscopy
bullets: CSF reaction (pH) is determined with diagnostic test strips; relative density is measured with a small hydrometer or a test strip — it can be raised in brain injury, meningitis, uraemia, diabetes and others.

Qualitative protein tests: Nonne–Apelt (with saturated ammonium sulfate; a whitish ring appears at the boundary of the layers) and Pandy (with saturated carbolic acid; a white cloud forms); the result is graded on a “4-plus” scale.

Microscopy is important in diagnosing inflammatory diseases of the nervous system, strokes, tumours and other processes; for an accurate result cells are counted within 30 minutes of obtaining the CSF.

slides.title: CSF biochemistry and microscopy
bullets: Leukocytes are stained with Samson’s reagent (it destroys erythrocytes and preserves leukocytes) and counted in the Goryaev chamber.
Erythrocytes: bloody CSF is diluted 9:1 with isotonic sodium chloride and counted in the Goryaev chamber.
The differential of cellular elements is also studied: in adults CSF cells are mainly lymphocytes and monocytes.

slides.title: Why is blood glucose needed when interpreting CSF glucose?
options: Blood glucose has no effect on CSF
Only to judge the safety of lumbar puncture
CSF glucose depends on blood glucose, so the two are compared
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. For example, high blood sugar raises CSF glucose.

Basis: MedlinePlus: CSF glucose should be more than two-thirds of blood glucose; blood glucose, especially extreme, affects the result.

slides.title: What is important in examining cerebrospinal fluid to prevent false erythrocytorrhachia:
options: Not taking the first 3–5 drops of CSF

slides.title: Clinical and diagnostic significance of cerebrospinal fluid examination?
bullets: 1. CSF examination is important in diagnosing meningitis, encephalitis, subarachnoid hemorrhage, demyelination and tumor metastases; opening pressure is measured at lumbar puncture.
2. Macroscopic: color and clarity (turbid – pleocytosis; red – blood; xanthochromia points to subarachnoid hemorrhage).

3. Cells: very few in the norm (mononuclears); bacterial meningitis – neutrophilic pleocytosis, high protein, low glucose; viral – lymphocytic pleocytosis (may be neutrophilic at first), normal glucose; tuberculous and fungal – lymphocytic, high protein, low glucose.

slides.title: Clinical and diagnostic significance of cerebrospinal fluid examination?
bullets: 4. Biochemistry: protein, glucose (compare with simultaneous blood glucose), lactate; microbiology: Gram, culture, antigens, PCR (viral and bacterial panels), cryptococcal antigen.
5. Cytology – tumor cells; oligoclonal bands (multiple sclerosis) – specialized laboratory.
6. Preanalytics: deliver the specimen immediately (cells disintegrate quickly), sterile containers, account for the effect of traumatic blood in the first tube.
